newsitem.title: USA: Damage at Bonneville Dam may cut output by 200 MW.
newsitem.headline: Damage at Bonneville Dam may cut output by 200 MW.

text.p: Damage to a fish ladder at Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River in Oregon could reduce power generation at the project by 200 megawatts (MW) for the next month or two, a spokeswoman for the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) said Friday.
The 1,147 MW project was damaged by debris, she noted.
Ideally, the dam's second powerhouse needs to be totally shut down during the repair work, but constraints related to the migration of endangered fish species rule that out, the spokeswoman said.
"If we shut the second powerhouse, the extra spill would raise the nitrogen content in the water to more than 120 percent," said BPA's Crystal Ball.
That is the threshold above which gas bubble disease is deemed harmful to the fish.
As a result, the repairs will be carried out with the powerhouse only partially curtailed and the situation will be closely monitored, BPA said.

In addition, there is some concern that slower flows through Bonneville Dam could cause streamflows to back up at the John Day "cut plain," where a main hub of the AC Pacific Intertie is located, Ball noted.
If that happens, capacity on the AC line would have to be reduced, although a "blanket" cutback will not be imposed, she said.

Meanwhile, final okay to lift capacity for the AC and DC segments of the Intertie remains on hold pending confirmation by a Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC) study group of necessary operating procedures, BPA said.
The WSCC approved this week a summer increase in the line's capacity to 6,900 MW from the current limit of 6,300 MW.
But that is "contingent on operating procedures being in place and on some operator training," Ball said.
The WSCC will meet Tuesday to discuss these issues and BPA is hopeful that final okay to raise the capacity will come by the end of next week, she added.
